deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::00 Map · Big Picture

fields.Front: Trace the chain from a probability \(p(x)\) to KL divergence, naming the operation at each step.
fields.Back:
probability \(p\) → take −log → surprise → average under p → entropy \(H(p)\) → take surprise from model q instead → cross-entropy \(H(p,q)\) → subtract H(p) → KL.
Side branches: exponentiate CE → perplexity; one-hot p → CE loss = NLL.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::00 Map · Big Picture

fields.Front: Many things are “just an expectation” \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\). Name 6 and their \(f\).
fields.Back:
• mean: \(f(x)=x\)
  • second moment: \(f(x)=x^2\)
  • variance: \(f(x)=(x-\mu)^2\)
  • MSE / ML loss: \(f=(\hat y-y)^2\) or any error \(\ell\)
  • entropy: \(f(x)=-\log p(x)\)
  • cross-entropy: \(f(x)=-\log q(x)\), averaged under \(p\)
  • covariance: \(f=(x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y)\)
fields.Extra: Once you can compute a weighted average, you can compute all of these.

fields.Front: Which four quantities all measure spread / uncertainty, and of what?
fields.Back:

  • MSE: spread of predictions around the targets
  • Surprise: how unexpected one outcome is
  • Entropy: average surprise, i.e. uncertainty of a whole distribution

fields.Front: Where does squaring show up, why, and how do we undo it?
fields.Back: Variance, MSE, L2 norm, RMS. Squaring makes every deviation positive (so they can't cancel) and punishes big deviations more. Taking the square root (std, RMS, ‖x‖) brings you back to the original units.

fields.Front: What are probability theory and information theory each for?
fields.Back:

Information theory: quantifying how much uncertainty a distribution contains.

fields.Problem: A coin has already been flipped and is covered by a hand. What's P(heads)? Which interpretation justifies your answer?
fields.Steps: The event is in the past, so the world isn't uncertain, but you are. For a Bayesian, probability measures what you know, not just what hasn't happened yet.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::01 Foundations · Interpretations & Vocabulary

fields.Front: What was the probability of rain in Paris on 1 March 1850? How do the two schools answer?
fields.Back:
Frequentist: it's a fixed one-off fact (0 or 1), not repeatable, so there's no meaningful probability.
Bayesian: you don't know, so assign a belief, e.g. the base rate of rainy March days (~40%).
fields.Extra: Same idea as the covered coin: already decided, still unknown to you.

fields.Front: One coin flip lands heads, so the likelihood is \(L(\theta) = \theta\). Compute \(\int_0^1 L(\theta)\,d\theta\). What does the result tell you about likelihood?
fields.Back: \(\tfrac12\), not 1 → likelihood is not a probability distribution over θ. It only ranks parameters: here θ = 1 explains “heads” best.
fields.Extra:
Contrast: fix θ = 0.7 and sum over the outcomes: P(H) + P(T) = 0.7 + 0.3 = 1.
What you hold fixed decides what sums to 1: θ fixed → probabilities over outcomes sum to 1; data fixed → likelihood over θ doesn't have to.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: What is a PMF? Give its two constraints.
fields.Back:
Probability mass function, for discrete variables: a probability for each outcome.
\(0 \le P(x) \le 1\) and \(\sum_x P(x) = 1\).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: What is a PDF? Give its constraints.
fields.Back: Probability density function, for continuous variables: \(p(x) \ge 0\) and \(\int p(x)\,dx = 1\). Probabilities are areas over ranges: \(P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b p(x)\,dx\).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: For a continuous height, why is P(X = 1.75 exactly) = 0? Does 0 mean impossible?
fields.Back: A single point has zero width, so it has zero area under the curve. Probability 0 ≠ impossible: some exact value always occurs. Probability lives in ranges, not points.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: Can a PDF value be greater than 1?
fields.Back: Yes. A density is not a probability. E.g. uniform on [0, 0.5] has density 2 everywhere. Only the area must be ≤ 1.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: Uniform distribution: discrete vs continuous formula?
fields.Back:
Discrete with k states: \(P(x) = 1/k\).
Continuous on [a, b]: \(p(x) = \dfrac{1}{b-a}\) (1/k makes no sense with infinitely many states).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Problem: X is uniform on [2, 6]. What's the density, and \(P(3 \le X \le 4)\)?
fields.Steps: Density = 1/(b − a) = 1/(6 − 2) = 0.25. Area of the range = width × height = 1 × 0.25 = 0.25.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Problem: Roll two fair dice. What is P(sum = 7)?
fields.Steps: Total outcomes: 6 × 6 = 36. Pairs summing to 7: (1,6) (2,5) (3,4) (4,3) (5,2) (6,1) = 6. 7 is the mode of the sum.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Problem: Two dice: P(sum = 2)? P(sum ≥ 10)?
fields.Steps: Only (1,1) gives 2. Sums 10, 11, 12 have 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 combinations.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: What is the joint probability \(P(x, y)\)?
fields.Back: The probability that x and y both happen.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: Intuitively, what does marginalising out y do?
fields.Back: It collapses a joint table into one variable. E.g. from a table of P(weather, traffic), get P(weather) by adding up each row over all traffic levels.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Text: Product rule: {{c1::\( P(x, y) = P(y \mid x)\,P(x) \)}}

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Text: Chain rule: {{c1::\( P(a, b, c) = P(a)\,P(b \mid a)\,P(c \mid a, b) \)}}
fields.Extra: General: \(P(x_1..x_n)=\prod_i P(x_i\mid x_1..x_{i-1})\). A joint distribution decomposes into a chain of conditionals.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Front: Where does the chain rule show up in LLMs?
fields.Back: A language model scores a sentence as \(P(\text{sentence}) = \prod_t P(\text{token}_t \mid \text{previous tokens})\). That long product is why we work in log space (sum of log-probs).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::02 Distributions & Rules

fields.Text: Independence: {{c1::\( P(x, y) = P(x)\,P(y) \)}}, equivalently {{c2::\( P(x \mid y) = P(x) \)}}.

fields.Text: Conditional independence given z: {{c1::\( P(x, y \mid z) = P(x \mid z)\,P(y \mid z) \)}}

fields.Front: Give an example of two variables that are dependent but conditionally independent given a third.
fields.Back: Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated, but (roughly) independent once you condition on temperature, the common cause.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Extra: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: Name the four parts of Bayes' rule \(P(A\mid B) = P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B)\).
fields.Back:
• \(P(A)\): prior, belief before the evidence
  • \(P(B\mid A)\): likelihood, how well the idea predicts the evidence
  • \(P(B)\): evidence / normaliser, how common the evidence is overall
  • \(P(A\mid B)\): posterior, updated belief

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: In one sentence, what is Bayes' rule for?
fields.Back: To flip a conditional: you know P(evidence | idea) but want P(idea | evidence).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: Derive Bayes' rule from the product rule.
fields.Back: \(P(A,B) = P(A\mid B)P(B) = P(B\mid A)P(A)\). Divide both sides by \(P(B)\).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: What's the counting way to think about Bayes?
fields.Back: Imagine 1,000 cases. Zoom into the group that matches the evidence, then ask what share of them has the outcome you care about.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: Name 4 real situations where you reach for Bayes' rule.
fields.Back: Whenever the evidence is easy to measure but you care about the cause: medical tests, spam filters (“free” → spam?), fraud detection, hiring tests, AI-text detectors.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: What is the base-rate effect (base-rate fallacy)?
fields.Back: When the thing you're looking for is rare, even an accurate test's false positives (from the huge negative group) can swamp the true positives. Always ask how rare it is before trusting a test.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Problem: 1,000 startups: 50 succeed. 100 have repeat founders, and 20 of the 50 winners had repeat founders. P(success | repeat founder)?
fields.Steps:
P(A) = 0.05, P(B) = 0.10, P(B|A) = 20/50 = 0.40.
\(0.40 \times 0.05 / 0.10 = 0.20\). Counts check: 20 of the 100 repeat-founder startups succeeded.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Problem: 1,000 essays, 100 written by AI. A detector catches 90% of AI essays and wrongly flags 10% of human ones. An essay is flagged: P(AI)?
fields.Hint: False-positive rate applies to the 900 humans only.
fields.Steps:
AI flagged: 0.9 × 100 = 90. Human flagged: 0.1 × 900 = 90. Flagged total 180. P(AI | flagged) = 90/180 = 0.5.
Formula: 0.9 × 0.1 / 0.18 = 0.5.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Problem: Same detector (90% catch, 10% false flags), but only 1% of 1,000 essays are AI. P(AI | flagged)?
fields.Steps: AI: 10 essays → 9 flagged. Humans: 990 → 99 flagged. Flagged = 108. 9/108 ≈ 0.083. Rarer target → false positives dominate even more.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: Most common slip in Bayes count problems?
fields.Back: Applying an error rate to the wrong group. The false-positive rate applies only to the negatives (10% of the 900 humans = 90, not 100).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::03 Bayes' Rule

fields.Front: Startup example: prior 5%, then you learn the founders built two successful companies before. Which part is prior, evidence, posterior? What's the main criticism?
fields.Back: Prior = 5% base rate; evidence = track record; posterior ≈ 20%. Criticism: priors can be subjective. Bayes' rule at least makes the update consistent maths instead of gut feel.

fields.Front: Why is \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_x P(x)\,x\) “the mean”?
fields.Back: A sample average is \(\sum \text{value} \times \frac{\text{count}}{N}\). As N grows, count/N → P(x), so the average → \(\sum P(x)\,x\). E[X] is the mean, defined for a distribution instead of a list.

fields.Front: Why do we square the distances in variance?
fields.Back: The plain average distance from the mean is always 0 (positives and negatives cancel). Squaring makes every distance positive and weighs big deviations more.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::04 Expectation · Variance · Std

fields.Front: Units of variance? What do we do about it?
fields.Back: Squared units (minutes², k$²), which are hard to interpret. Take the square root to get the standard deviation, back in original units.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::04 Expectation · Variance · Std
Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::04 Expectation · Variance · Std

fields.Front: What does a standard deviation tell you in practice?
fields.Back: The typical distance of an outcome from the mean. It's a measure of risk / consistency: same average, different predictability (delivery apps, investments).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::04 Expectation · Variance · Std

fields.Front: Why do maths texts prefer variance and practitioners std?
fields.Back: Variance has nicer algebra: easy to differentiate (no square root), and it adds for independent variables (\(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}X+\mathrm{Var}Y\)). Std is interpretable in original units.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::04 Expectation · Variance · Std

fields.Problem: Game A always pays 5. Game B pays 0 or 10, 50/50. Mean and variance of each?
fields.Steps: B: E[X²] = (0 + 100)/2 = 50; 50 − 5² = 25. Same average, B is spread out.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::04 Expectation · Variance · Std

fields.Problem: App A delivers in 28 or 32 min (50/50); App B in 10 or 50 min (50/50). Variance and std of each?
fields.Answer: A: Var 4 min², σ 2 min. B: Var 400 min², σ 20 min.
fields.Steps: Both means are 30. A: every delivery is 2 away → 2² = 4. B: every delivery is 20 away (20 early or 20 late) → 400. σ = 20 means “typically 20 min off the average”.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::04 Expectation · Variance · Std

fields.Front: Two classic slips when computing a weighted variance?
fields.Back:
1. Forgetting the weights: 25 + 25 = 50 is wrong; it's 0.5·25 + 0.5·25 = 25.
  2. Wrong order: it's \(P(x)\cdot(x-\mu)^2\), not \((P(x)\cdot(x-\mu))^2\). Square first, then weight.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::05 Mode & Median

fields.Front: Define the mode of a distribution.
fields.Back: The most probable value (highest P), not the biggest value.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::05 Mode & Median

fields.Front: Define the median of a distribution.
fields.Back: Sort outcomes by value, accumulate probability, and take the value where the cumulative probability first reaches 0.5.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::05 Mode & Median

fields.Problem: Sign-ups: 0 (0.2), 5 (0.5), 10 (0.3). Mode, median, mean?
fields.Steps: Mode: biggest probability is 0.5 at 5. Median: 0.2 at 0, then 0.7 at 5, which crosses 0.5. Mean is pulled up by the 10-sign-up days.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::05 Mode & Median

fields.Problem: Values 2, 5, 3, each with probability 1/3. Median?
fields.Steps: Sort by value: 2, 3, 5. Cumulative: 0.33, 0.67 → 3 crosses 0.5. Listing order doesn't matter.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::05 Mode & Median

fields.Front: Which of mean / median / mode work for names or colours, and why?
fields.Back: Only the mode. The median needs an order, and the mean needs numbers. The mode only asks which is most common.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::05 Mode & Median

fields.Front: Why can the mean differ from the median?
fields.Back: Skew: the mean gets pulled toward a long tail or toward big values, while the median only cares about the halfway point.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: What does “normalized” mean? Give 5 example constraints.
fields.Back: Data transformed to satisfy a constraint: Σ = 1, range [0, 1], μ = 0 & σ = 1, length ‖x‖ = 1, max = 1.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: What are the two families of normalization?
fields.Back:
Probability normalization: make a valid distribution (divide by sum, softmax).
Scale normalization: centre and/or rescale values (z-score / LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Problem: Scores [2, 1, 1]. Normalise by (a) dividing by the sum, (b) softmax.
fields.Steps: Softmax: e² ≈ 7.39, e¹ ≈ 2.72; sum ≈ 12.83 → 0.576, 0.212, 0.212. The leader gains share: softmax amplifies gaps.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: What is softmax's shift invariance, and why does it hold?
fields.Back: \(\mathrm{softmax}(x + c) = \mathrm{softmax}(x)\): the factor \(e^c\) appears in numerator and denominator and cancels. Only differences between logits matter. [12, 11, 11] gives the same 0.58/0.21/0.21; dividing by the sum would give 0.35/0.32/0.32.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: Why does every implementation subtract max(x) before softmax?
fields.Back: It gives the same result (shift invariance) and prevents overflow from things like \(e^{1000}\).

fields.Front: Why is it called softmax?
fields.Back: It's a smooth, differentiable version of argmax: the biggest logit takes most of the probability, yet gradients still reach every option.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: Why softmax instead of just dividing scores by their sum? (3 reasons)
fields.Back:
1. Handles negative scores: \(e^x > 0\) always.
  2. Smooth and easy to differentiate.
  3. Pairs with cross-entropy: the log cancels the exp, giving gradient = prediction − target.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: Does softmax make distributions truly sparse?
fields.Back: No. \(e^x > 0\) means no output is ever exactly 0, so “peaked” or “low-entropy” is more accurate. For true zeros, see sparsemax.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: Derive the gradient of cross-entropy loss through softmax (target index i).
fields.Back: \(-\log \mathrm{softmax}(x)_i = -x_i + \log\sum_j e^{x_j}\). Differentiate w.r.t. \(x_j\): \(\mathrm{softmax}(x)_j - \mathbb{1}[j=i]\) = prediction − one-hot target.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: Why do we need scale normalization at all? (features + deep nets)
fields.Back:
Features: house size (~2,000 sq ft) would drown out bedrooms (~3) purely because of units. Standardising puts every feature on a level playing field.
Deep nets: values passing through many layers drift and blow up or shrink. Normalising keeps each layer in a steady range, so training stays stable.

fields.Front: What question does a z-score answer, and how does it reframe the value?
fields.Back: “How many standard deviations is this from the mean?” It changes “how big is it?” into “how unusual is it compared with its group?”

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: What does centring (subtracting the mean) achieve, and when is it useful?
fields.Back: It measures values relative to the group average, which removes a shared offset (e.g. everyone's scores bumped by an easy exam). In networks, values balanced around 0 keep gradients well behaved; all-positive inputs make weight updates zig-zag.

fields.Front: LayerNorm vs classic standardization: same formula, different axis. Explain.
fields.Back:
Classic: normalise each feature across samples in the dataset.
LayerNorm: normalise across the features of one sample (e.g. the 768 dims of a single token), using that token's own μ and σ. Plus learned γ, β and ε.

fields.Front: RMSNorm vs LayerNorm: the key difference and why it's used.
fields.Back: RMSNorm drops centring (no mean subtraction, no β) and only rescales. The rescaling does most of the stabilising work, so it's cheaper and simpler and performs about as well in practice (not mathematically equal). Used in Llama and other big LLMs.

fields.Front: L2 normalization keeps what and discards what? When do you use it?
fields.Back: Keeps direction, discards length. Used when comparing embeddings (cosine similarity), where you care which way they point, not how big they are.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: How are RMS and the L2 norm related? What does each normalization produce?
fields.Back: \(\mathrm{RMS}(x) = \lVert x\rVert_2 / \sqrt{n}\). After L2: the vector's total length is 1. After RMSNorm: each entry is about 1 in size on average.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: Invariances: which of softmax / LayerNorm / RMSNorm ignore shifting the input? Scaling it?
fields.Back:
• Softmax: shift-invariant, scale-sensitive
  • LayerNorm: invariant to both (subtracts mean, divides by σ)
  • RMSNorm: scale-invariant, not shift-invariant (no centring)

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::06 Normalization · Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, L2

fields.Front: Explain softmax as you would in an interview.
fields.Back:
1. What it does. A probability normalization (not a scale one like LayerNorm, RMSNorm or L2): it turns any real-valued scores (logits) into a distribution. Every output is > 0 and they sum to 1.

2. Formula. Exponentiate, then divide by the sum; temperature divides the logits first: \[\mathrm{softmax}(x)_i = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}, \qquad \mathrm{softmax}(x/T)\] 3. Compared with dividing by the sum, \(x_i / \sum_j x_j\):
Divide by the sumSoftmax
Inputsmust be ≥ 0 (breaks on negatives or a zero sum)any real numbers
What mattersratios: \(p_i/p_j = x_i/x_j\)differences: \(p_i/p_j = e^{x_i - x_j}\)
Add a constantchanges the outputno change (shift-invariant)
Multiply by a constantno change (scale-invariant)changes the output (scale-sensitive)
Gapskeeps proportionsamplifies them; the leader gains share

4. Key properties
  • Shift invariance: \(e^c\) cancels top and bottom, so implementations subtract \(\max(x)\) first to avoid overflow (\(e^{1000}\)).
  • Temperature: T → 0 approaches argmax (one-hot); T → ∞ approaches uniform.
  • Soft argmax: smooth, differentiable, order-preserving. \(\partial p_i/\partial x_j = p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j)\).
  • Never exactly 0 (\(e^x > 0\)): peaked, not sparse. Sparsemax gives true zeros.
  • With cross-entropy: \(\log \mathrm{softmax}(x)_i = x_i - \mathrm{logsumexp}(x)\), so the gradient is prediction − one-hot target.
  • Two classes reduce to the sigmoid: \(\mathrm{softmax}([a, 0])_1 = \sigma(a)\).
5. Example: logits [2, 1, 1]
  • Divide by the sum: 0.50 / 0.25 / 0.25
  • Softmax: e² ≈ 7.39, e ≈ 2.72, sum ≈ 12.83 → 0.576 / 0.212 / 0.212
  • Shift +10 → [12, 11, 11]: softmax unchanged; divide-by-sum gives 0.35 / 0.32 / 0.32
  • Scale ×10 → [20, 10, 10]: softmax ≈ 0.9999 / 0.00005 / 0.00005; divide-by-sum unchanged
fields.Extra:
Where it shows up: the last layer of classifiers and of LLMs picking the next token, attention weights \(\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})\), RL policies \(\pi(a \mid s)\).
Grade: all 5 parts → Good · one missing → Hard · two or more missing → Again.

fields.Front: How do you read the sign of covariance?
fields.Back: + move together (above-average X with above-average Y); − move in opposite directions; ≈ 0 no linear relationship.

fields.Front: Units of covariance? Why is its magnitude hard to read?
fields.Back: (unit of X) × (unit of Y), e.g. hours × points. Probabilities have no units. Measuring hours in minutes multiplies Cov by 60 although the relationship is unchanged.

fields.Front: Relationship between variance and covariance?
fields.Back: \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathrm{Cov}(X, X)\)

fields.Front: Independent ⇒ Cov = 0. Does Cov = 0 ⇒ independent?
fields.Back: No. Covariance only detects linear patterns. An inverted-U relationship can have Cov ≈ 0 and still be strongly dependent.

fields.Problem: (X, Y) takes values (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), each with probability 1/3. Compute Cov and ρ.
fields.Steps: μX = 2, μY = 4. Products: (−1)(−2) = 2, 0, (1)(2) = 2 → mean 4/3. σX = √(2/3), σY = √(8/3), product = 4/3 → ρ = 1 (perfectly linear).

fields.Front: What is “the loss” conceptually, and what does training do with it?
fields.Back: The expected error of the model with its current settings. Training nudges the weights to lower it, re-measures, and repeats. You choose the error function ℓ to suit the problem.

fields.Front: Bits vs nats? Convert between them.
fields.Back:
Same quantity, different units: bits use \(\log_2\); nats use \(\ln\) (base e).
1 nat ≈ 1.44 bits; 1 bit = ln 2 ≈ 0.693 nats. Changing the base rescales every number by a constant, so it never changes which model is best.

fields.Front: Why does ML default to nats?
fields.Back: \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = 1/x\) (no extra constant), and ln cancels the e in softmax, which gives the clean “prediction − target” gradient.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::09 Information Theory · Surprise, Entropy, CE, KL, Perplexity

fields.Front: Why do we use log-probabilities in ML? (3 reasons)
fields.Back:
1. Numerical stability: multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0; adding logs stays manageable.
  2. Easier gradients: sums are simpler to differentiate than long products; log is monotonic, so the argmax is unchanged.
  3. Surprise adds up: log turns × into +, and base 2 counts yes/no questions.

fields.Front: Why does \(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\)?
fields.Back: Exponents add when you multiply powers: \(2^3 \cdot 2^2 = 2^5\). A log returns the exponent, so the log of a product is the sum of the exponents.

fields.Front: What does “log is monotonic” mean, and why does it matter?
fields.Back: If a > b then log a > log b. So maximising log p finds the same answer as maximising p.

fields.Back: No: \(D_{KL} \ge 0\) (Gibbs' inequality). So \(H(p,q) \ge H(p)\): a model can't be less surprised than the truth on average, which puts a floor on perplexity.

fields.Front: Is KL symmetric? Illustrate with a 1% event.
fields.Back:
No, \(D(p\Vert q) \ne D(q\Vert p)\).
Truth 1%, model 0% → when it happens, \(-\log 0 = \infty\): catastrophic.
Truth 0%, model 1% → it never happens, so you only lose the wasted 1%: cheap.

fields.Front: Why do trained models (almost) never assign exactly 0 to any token?
fields.Back: Softmax can't output 0 (\(e^x > 0\)). A never-seen token gets pushed lower and lower, but stays > 0, which protects against an infinite loss if it ever appears.

fields.Front: Why is minimising cross-entropy loss the same as MLE?
fields.Back: CE loss = average of \(-\log\) (probability the model gave the real data). MLE = make those probabilities as high as possible. Pushing probabilities up = pushing minus their log down. It's the same goal; the minus sign exists because frameworks minimise.

fields.Problem: 10 flips, 7 heads. Compare \(L(0.5)\) and \(L(0.7)\). Which does MLE pick?
fields.Answer: θ = 0.7, which explains the data ≈ 2.28× better.
fields.Steps:
\(L(\theta) = \theta^7(1-\theta)^3\) (the binomial coefficient cancels when comparing).
L(0.5) = 0.5¹⁰ ≈ 0.000977; L(0.7) = 0.7⁷·0.3³ ≈ 0.002224.

fields.Front: How does a prior fix MLE's overfitting? Name the estimator and its ML counterpart.
fields.Back: MAP: maximise likelihood × prior (Bayes: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior). A prior that says “coins are usually near fair” stops θ jumping to 1. In ML, regularisation (e.g. weight decay ≈ Gaussian prior) plays this role.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: \(\ln x\) answers “\(e\) to what power gives \(x\)?” Given \(e^{0.69} \approx 2\), what is \(\ln 0.5\)?
fields.Steps: 0.5 < 1, so the power is negative: \(e^{-0.69} = 1/e^{0.69} = 1/2\). So \(\ln 0.5 = -\ln 2\). Halving a probability subtracts 0.69 in log space.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: A model gives a token log-prob \(-2.3\). Given \(e^{2.3} \approx 10\), what is the probability?
fields.Steps: \(e^{-2.3} = 1/e^{2.3} \approx 1/10\). Each further \(-2.3\) is another factor of 10 smaller: \(-4.6 \to 0.01\), \(-6.9 \to 0.001\).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: \(\log_2 0.125 = ?\) What is it counting?
fields.Steps: \(2^{-3} = 1/8 = 0.125\). A log counts how many times you multiply by the base; a negative log counts halvings from 1. Any probability < 1 has a negative log.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: You add \(0.69\) to a logit \(x\). What happens to \(e^{x}\)?
fields.Steps: \(e^{x + 0.69} = e^{x}\, e^{0.69} = 2e^{x}\). Adding in log space = multiplying in probability space.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: A 3-token sequence has token probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.5. Compute \(\log_2\) of the sequence probability as one product, then as a sum of logs.
fields.Steps: Product: \(0.5 \cdot 0.25 \cdot 0.5 = 1/16 \Rightarrow \log_2 = -4\). Sum: \((-1) + (-2) + (-1) = -4\). \(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\), which is why models add log-probs.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: A 1000-token answer where every token has \(p = 0.9\) (\(\ln 0.9 \approx -0.105\)). Total log-prob? Why not just multiply the probabilities?
fields.Steps: \(\ln(0.9^{1000}) = 1000 \ln 0.9 \approx -105\). The probability \(e^{-105} \approx 2\times10^{-46}\) is below float32’s smallest normal number (\(\sim10^{-38}\)): multiplying underflows to 0, summing logs doesn’t.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: \(\ln 8 \approx 2.08\) and \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69\). Use them to get \(\log_2 8\).
fields.Steps: Change of base: \(\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2 = 2.08 / 0.69 = 3\). Same move converts nats to bits.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: Attention scores are divided by \(\sqrt{d}\). For \(d = 64\), write the factor as a power of \(d\) and compute it.
fields.Steps: \(1/\sqrt{d} = d^{-1/2}\): a root is a fractional power, dividing is a negative power. \(64^{1/2} = 8\), so \(64^{-1/2} = 1/8\).

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: The learning rate halves every epoch. By what factor has it shrunk after 10 epochs (as a power, and roughly as a number)?
fields.Steps: Ten factors of \(1/2\): \((2^{-1})^{10} = 2^{-10} = 1/1024\). Exponents add when you multiply powers of the same base.

deck: Math4ML::Probability & Information Theory::11 Algebra · Powers & Logs

fields.Problem: One coin flip lands heads, so the log-likelihood is \(\ln\theta\). What is its gradient at \(\theta = 0.25\), and which way does gradient ascent move \(\theta\)?
fields.Steps: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\ln\theta = 1/\theta\). Small \(\theta\) → big gradient: the less likely the data under the model, the harder the push toward explaining it.
